pedagogy.summary: At 6-8, sorting matures into ORGANISING and RECORDING data: given a question, sort items into 2-3 categories, count each, and capture the result as a simple table or list of category-names-with-counts, then order the categories. The shift from the 5-6 skill is that the count is now written down as a record that can be read back to answer the question — the beginning of GAISE's data sense (data are information about a context). Teaching should start from a genuine question ('which packed-lunch fruit is most popular?'), collect and tally, transfer to a table, and always return to the question so the table is a tool, not a decoration.
bestPractices: Begin with a statistical question worth asking, so the organised data has a purpose to answer
Model the tally-then-table pipeline: sort/tally the raw data, then write each category name beside its count in a table or list
Keep category totals reconciling with the whole set ('7 + 5 + 4 = 16, and we had 16 cards') to build a self-check habit
Read the table back to answer the question and to order the categories most-to-fewest
keyRepresentations: Simple frequency table / list (category name + count)
Sorted objects or cards arranged in rows as the concrete source
Ordered list of categories from most to fewest
commonMisconceptions: Records counts that don't line up with their categories (rows misaligned in the table)
Organises the data but cannot read it back to answer the original question (table treated as decoration)
Miscounts categories or the totals don't reconcile with the full set
Forces every item into the given categories (or invents overlaps) when some items fit none

learn.summary: For ages 6-8, sorting matures into organising AND recording categorical data: starting from a genuine statistical question, children sort items into 2-3 categories, count each, write each category name beside its count in a simple table or list, and order the categories by quantity. The new skill beyond the 5-6 level is that the count becomes a written record that can be read back to answer the question — the table is a tool, not a decoration. Teaching should begin from a real question (e.g. 'which packed-lunch fruit is most popular?'), collect and tally, transfer to a table with totals that reconcile against the whole set, and always return to the question.

activities.title: Survey organiser: from response cards to a table that answers the question
feedback: If row counts don't add up to the number of cards, a card may have been lost or double-counted — recount by moving each card aside as it is tallied, and check the parts sum to the whole
If asked 'which does the class like best?' and the child re-counts cards instead of reading the table, model reading it: 'the biggest number is beside…' and return to the question
If a card fits none of the given categories, don't force it into a pile — allow an 'other' category if genuinely needed
Point to each pile and its matching table row together as the number is written, so counts and labels stay correctly paired
activities.rationale: Organising categorical data is a procedural build-it task: sorting raw cards and watching a table populate makes the tally-then-table pipeline concrete and gives immediate feedback. Ordering the rows makes the answer surface, reinforcing that data are collected to answer a question about a context.
sourceClaims: At Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable using tables and picture/bar graphs and develop 'data sense' — that data are information collected to answer a statistical investigative question about a context
Year 2 pupils interpret and construct simple tables and sort categories by quantity, asking and answering questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
learnerActions: Start from a real question the class cares about, e.g. 'which of these three snacks is most popular?' or 'which of these three fruits does our class like best?'
Take a shuffled stack of class response cards and sort each card into one of 2-3 categories, building a tally as you go
Write each category name beside its count in a simple table or list
Check that the row counts add up to the number of cards you started with (e.g. '7 + 5 + 4 = 16, and we had 16 cards')
Order the categories from most to fewest so the category with the biggest count rises to the top (if two categories have the same biggest count, say that they are tied rather than naming one winner)
Read the table back aloud to state which category answers the question

Test the table as a live record: if two more children chose one fruit, update that count, check that the new total is 2 more than before (e.g. 18 instead of 16), and see whether the ordered answer changes
activities.intendedInsight: An organised table is a tool that ANSWERS a question, not just a store of numbers: once ordered, the record visibly shows the most popular category, the totals should reconcile with the whole set, and updating a count updates the answer.

activities.title: Interactive reconcile-and-order check (optional self-check mechanism)
feedback: A reconcile flag when totals don't match the card count makes a lost or double-counted response visible — treat it as a prompt to recount, not a failure
When 'order' is pressed the rows re-rank most-to-fewest so the most popular category rises to the top, showing the answer emerging from the data itself
activities.rationale: Optional interactive mechanisms (drag-to-sort, a tally that builds, a count cell that checks against the raw data, an 'order' control) make the recording-and-reconciling of a constructed table concrete and give feedback as each count is entered. These are illustrative affordances, not required tools — the same pipeline of constructing a table and sorting categories by quantity works with physical cards and a paper table.
sourceClaims: Year 2 pupils interpret and construct simple tables and sort categories by quantity, asking and answering questions about totalling and comparing categorical data
learnerActions: Drag each response card to a category pile and watch a tally build
Type each count into a table's cells
Notice when the row counts are flagged for not reconciling with the number of cards, and fix the lost or double-counted response
Press an 'order' control and watch the rows rank themselves most-to-fewest, lifting the winning category to the top
Answer a final question — which category answers our question?
activities.intendedInsight: A live record stays trustworthy only when its parts reconcile with the whole; ordering the rows turns the record into a visible answer.

activities.title: Read a completed table to say what it means (annotation scaffold)
feedback: If the child reads a count without naming its category, re-pair the label and number together
This reference-only reading supports interpretation but does not itself practise organising raw data — pair it with a hands-on sort so the child also builds the table
activities.rationale: A labelled, static table can teach interpretation (what each row means, which is largest) as a reference scaffold. It is a complement to, not a replacement for, the build-it task, because it does not let the child organise raw data into a table.
sourceClaims: At Level A students represent the distribution of a categorical variable using tables and picture/bar graphs and develop 'data sense' — that data are information collected to answer a statistical investigative question about a context
learnerActions: Look at a completed, labelled frequency table of category names and counts
Point to each row and say what it means ('this row says 5 children chose banana')
Say which row has the biggest count and what question that answers
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a table back — pairing each label with its count and identifying the largest — is a necessary step toward using data to answer a question.

constraints: Begin from a genuine statistical question so the organised data has a purpose to answer; always return to the question so the table is a tool, not a decoration
Model the full tally-then-table pipeline: sort/tally raw data, then write each category name beside its count
Build a reconcile habit: category totals should sum back to the whole set, and this self-check should be modelled explicitly
Limit to 2-3 categories with counts within young children's secure cardinality

Allow an 'other' category for items that fit none of the given categories, rather than forcing or double-placing them; keep the total number of categories, including 'other', within the 2-3 category limit (e.g. two named categories plus 'other')
The reading/annotation scaffold assesses and supports interpretation but does not elicit independent construction of a table from raw data; pair it with hands-on organising
Interactive reconcile/order controls are illustrative affordances; the same learning can occur with physical cards and a paper table — do not treat the digital tool as mandatory
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source row asserts '3D adds no value' and that conversation 'offers nothing to sort or tabulate'; these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws. They are omitted as universal claims — spoken discussion can still support framing the question and reading a table back, even if it is not the primary medium for the recording procedure.
An earlier candidate feedback line claimed 'live recolouring' of rows; this was not in the source and has been removed, leaving only the supported re-ranking behaviour.

The KS1 source claim is retained on the interactive activity only because that activity genuinely rehearses constructing a table and sorting categories by quantity; it is not evidence that the interactive medium outperforms paper, which remains an untested affordance.
The original assessment's gap/partial/full response tiers are not reproduced verbatim but are reflected in the feedback's distinction between supported and independent performance.
Prerequisite reteach links from the source (secure cardinality; clean non-overlapping sorting) are noted here as teaching dependencies but are not learner-facing citations.
The arithmetic example '7 + 5 + 4 = 16' checks out and is retained as a reconcile illustration.

probeDeeper: Ask 'do your table numbers add up to how many cards we started with?' to check the reconcile habit
Ask 'which fruit does the class like best — how does your table show that?' to see if the record is used to answer the question
Counterexample tuned to this topic: slip in a card for a fruit that isn't one of the three and watch whether they force it or handle it as 'other'
Ask 'if two more people chose apple, what changes in your table — and does the answer change?' to test that the table is a live record
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: sorts all cards into the three fruit categories, counts each, writes each fruit name beside its correct count in a table (totals reconciling with the number of cards), orders the categories, and states which fruit answers the question.

errorPatterns.pattern: Records counts that don't line up with their categories — the table's numbers and labels are mismatched
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the transfer — point to each pile and its row together as the number is written; a recording slip, so steady the pipeline rather than reteach sorting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The count written for a fruit doesn't match the pile the child actually made for it

errorPatterns.pattern: Organises the data but cannot read it back to answer the original question (table as decoration)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model reading a table to answer a question ('the biggest number is beside…'); keep returning to the question so the table becomes a tool
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'so which fruit does the class like best?' the child re-counts cards or shrugs instead of reading the table

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts a category or the totals don't reconcile with the full set (insecure cardinality)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rebuild cardinality — move each card aside as counted and check the parts sum to the whole
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Row counts don't sum to the number of cards, and a recount gives a different figure

errorPatterns.pattern: Forces cards that fit no category into a group, or double-places ambiguous ones, because the categorisation isn't kept clean
errorPatterns.nextMove: Revisit clean, non-overlapping sorting from the earlier skill; allow an 'other' category if genuinely needed
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A 'neither' card is jammed into a pile, or an item appears counted twice

responseLevels.gap: Sorts unreliably, mis-pairs or miscounts in the table, and cannot answer the question from it
responseLevels.full: Independently sorts, records reconciling counts correctly paired to categories, orders them, and reads the table back to answer the question
responseLevels.partial: Produces a table with correct counts when supported, but totals may not reconcile or the child re-counts rather than reading the table to answer

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Our question is: which of these three fruits does our class like best? Here are everyone's choice cards. Organise them so we can answer the question, and show me the counts in a table. (Set the task and WATCH how they organise and record.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Observing the organising-and-recording shows what a verbal answer hides. A child with the skill produces a table whose counts are correctly paired and reconcile, and reads it back to answer the question; a child without it mis-pairs counts, loses cards, or organises the data yet cannot use it to answer 'which best'.
